note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — TRACE THE LOW STEMS
tiles.details: Panels 1–2 show slender stems with short side-pointing blades. Nimblewill often sprawls and roots at its lower nodes, but an ordinary stem joint does not prove root emergence. Virginia Tech distinguishes reclining rooting culms from the more obvious long surface stolons of bermudagrass; avoid requiring a textbook runner. No current panel proves a root emerging from a node.
tiles.short: Low weak, branching perennial; inspect actual lower nodes for roots.
tiles.status: REAL LEAF/STEM PHOTO — ROOTED NODE MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · EXPOSE THE TRUE INNER LIGULE
tiles.details: World Flora Online reports 0.1–0.2 mm in one treatment; Ohio State and Go Botany report approximately 0.2–0.5 mm. Open a fresh attached blade/sheath junction with 10–20× magnification and 1-mm calibration. It is a short membrane with a fringed/erose edge, NOT simply bermudagrass's hair-fringe ligule. Existing photos do not resolve the membrane boundary.
tiles.short: Minute MEMBRANOUS, ciliolate ligule: roughly 0.1–0.5 mm across treatments.

tiles.heading: 03 · FIND THE NARROW FLOWERING PANICLE
tiles.details: The archived Emily Summerbell flowering photo (panel 3) actually shows a narrow head and leaf blade, with two prior gross arrows. Ohio State describes terminal/axillary contracted panicles 5–15 cm long; Go Botany 3–15 cm. Short appressed branches carry the spikelets. Do not call the entire panicle an unbranched spike or infer exact dimensions without a ruler.
tiles.short: Contracted, spike-like PANICLE about 3–15 cm; not digitate terminal fingers.
tiles.status: REAL FLOWERING PHOTO — NO MEASURED BRANCH DISSECTION

tiles.heading: 04 · INSPECT TINY GLUMES
tiles.details: Go Botany reports spikelets 1.8–2.8 mm. The lower glume is often rudimentary or absent; the upper glume is only about 0.1–0.3 mm (Ohio State, WFO). These are not the larger, more conspicuous glumes of many other muhlys. Photograph a ripe spikelet at 20–40× with a true millimeter scale and show glume attachment before assigning labels.
tiles.short: One fertile floret; spikelet roughly 1.8–2.8 mm; glumes nearly absent.

tiles.heading: 05 · SEPARATE THE LEMMA, CALLUS AND AWN
tiles.details: Ohio State gives a roughly 2-mm lemma and 2–5-mm tip awn; WFO describes 1.5–2-mm lemmas with 1.5–4-mm awns; Go Botany reports 1.5–5-mm awns. Examine the hairy floret callus, actual lemma tip/awn attachment and palea. No existing photo supports a micro-arrow or a direct millimeter measurement of these parts.
tiles.short: Three-veined lemma ~1.5–2.5 mm, terminal awn ~1.5–5 mm.

tiles.heading: 06 · BERMUDA AND APAREJO COMPARISON + RELEASE GATE
tiles.details: Bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) has fingerlike terminal racemes and a true fringe-of-hairs ligule; its stolons/rhizomes must be observed, not assumed. Aparejo muhly (M. utilis; comparison panel 4) needs separately proven underground scaly rhizomes, not inferred from fine leaves. M. lindheimeri is a much larger basal fountain. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same-plant rooted lower node, measured true ligule, ripe spikelet with nearly obsolete glumes and dissected awned lemma/callus, plus matched bermuda/aparejo anatomy. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify five existing local JPEGs, individual Emily Summerbell CC BY 4.0 and queenpossum CC BY-SA credits, four comparison panels, existing gross arrows and public mobile display. Retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
tiles.short: Nimblewill = reclining rooting nodes + narrow panicle + short membrane.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Look LOW: nimblewill forms thin, wiry, much-branched stems with short blades often spreading sideways from nodes. Trace one slender SURFACE stolon toward the ground and look for REAL roots coming from its lower nodes; a leaf/stem joint alone is NOT evidence of roots. When flowering, look for an exceptionally NARROW contracted spikelet-bearing panicle (not bermudagrass's fingerlike terminal spikes). Carefully open a fresh blade–sheath junction: nimblewill has a minute membranous, often uneven/ciliolate ligule; bermudagrass has a fringe of hairs instead. If rooting, ligule and seedhead are hidden, leave at Muhlenbergia sp. until confirmed.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Begin with current real nimblewill image 1: point out short leaf blades and actual LEAF/STEM attachment points on upright wiry branches. These are not yet photographed as rooted.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: World Flora Online reports 0.1–0.2 mm in one treatment; Ohio State and Go Botany report approximately 0.2–0.5 mm. Open a fresh attached blade/sheath junction with 10–20× magnification and 1-mm calibration. It is a short membrane with a fringed/erose edge, NOT simply bermudagrass's hair-fringe ligule. Existing photos do not resolve the membrane boundary.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: The archived Emily Summerbell flowering photo (panel 3) actually shows a narrow head and leaf blade, with two prior gross arrows. Ohio State describes terminal/axillary contracted panicles 5–15 cm long; Go Botany 3–15 cm. Short appressed branches carry the spikelets. Do not call the entire panicle an unbranched spike or infer exact dimensions without a ruler.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Nimblewill (M. schreberi) has slender above-ground stolons capable of ROOTING AT THE NODES, short sideways leaves, and narrow contracted terminal/axillary panicles. Bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) also has stolons, but produces several fingerlike racemes from a common tip and a HAIR FRINGE in place of the membranous ligule. Aparejo muhly (M. utilis) instead possesses BELOW-GROUND scaly RHIZOMES, very thin often rolled blades and tiny narrow heads; current appearjo photos DO NOT expose its rhizomes. Creeping bentgrass has a membranous but usually much longer ligule and a different open flowering structure. Kew describes a ciliate-edged membrane about 1 mm for nimblewill while regional flora/Ohio State descriptions include 0.1–0.5 mm: do not use one hard millimeter cutoff. Compare multiple characters. Preserve native-range checks as originally recorded.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

Arrows indicate visible collar location and ribbed sheath, not a verified 0.5-mm ligule.

panels.label: COMPARE ONLY · BERMUDAGRASS — real collar hair tufts
panels.caption: This is BERMUDAGRASS, not nimblewill. Pale hair tufts at the collar are genuinely visible beside a 2 mm photographed reference. Compare this hairy collar with nimblewill's very short membranous and often ragged/ciliolate INNER ligule, which still requires a calibrated source photo. Bermudagrass's hair tufts do not prove the identity of any unexamined low creeping grass.

panels.label: COMPARE ONLY · BERMUDAGRASS — digitate fingerlike seedhead
panels.caption: OTHER SPECIES, Cynodon dactylon, not nimblewill. This CC0 photograph contains source-baked identification arrows on a genuine finger-like terminal head with approximately five flowering racemes. Compare the radiating fingers to nimblewill's tight narrow panicle and awned spikelets. Digitate heads alone are not unique to bermudagrass.
